(1) the perianth–fruit gap in coconut fruits was significantly larger in the cultivar with the smallest and more elongated fruit, (2) in infested coconut fruits, the perianths were significantly wider and the perianth-flesh gap was significantly larger than in uninfested fruits and (3) the perianths of coconut fruits were significantly wider in the cultivar that was most infested by coconut fruit mites.

the gap between the coconut fruit periphery and the perianth rim is significantly different between cultivar and that the perianths of infested coconut fruit have a larger gap between the perianth surface and the fruit surface than the perianths on uninfested fruits.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the perianths of infested coconut fruit are more open to predatory mites than the perianths on uninfested coconut fruit.
the structure of coconut fruits changes in response to infestation by the coconut mite, and as a result, the perianths of infested coconut fruit become more accessible to its predators.
the coconut fruit peranths are not changed in response to infestation by coconut mites but the fruit itself expands in response to the infestation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the perianths of coconut fruits can be modified in response to infestation by coconut mites and as result, predators are able to move under the infested perianths and attack the coconut fruit.

coconut fruits respond to the damage caused by the eriophyoid pest, the coconut mite, by increasing the gap between the perianth rim and the fruit surface, thereby facilitating the entry of predatory mites.
the structure of coconut fruits changes as a result of damage by coconut mites.
